opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the key insight is that with a dataflow architecture, you're not thinking about the model as a sequence of individual kernels that you launch one after another, the way you would on a GPU. Instead, you look at the whole computation graph and ask: how do I spatially lay this out across the chip so that data streams from one operator to the next without going back out to memory?

On a conventional architecture, every kernel boundary is a round trip to HBM. You compute a matrix multiply, write the result out, read it back in for the activation or the normalization, write it out again, and so on. For inference, especially at the batch sizes people actually run in production, you end up memory-bandwidth bound. The compute units are sitting there waiting.

With our reconfigurable dataflow approach, the compiler takes the graph and fuses large portions of it, sometimes an entire transformer decoder layer, into a single pipelined configuration on the chip. The compute units and on-chip memory units are configured so that the output of one stage feeds directly into the next. You get pipeline parallelism within the chip, and the intermediate activations live in on-chip SRAM instead of going off-chip. That's where a lot of the speedup comes from, particularly for token generation, where you're doing relatively little compute per byte of weights you move.

So the mapping problem has a few dimensions. First is how you partition the graph, which operators to fuse together into one configuration, given the on-chip resources you have. Second is how you allocate compute and memory resources to each stage so the pipeline is balanced. If one stage is much slower, it becomes the bottleneck and everything else idles. Third is how you handle the memory hierarchy, and that's why we went to a three-tier design: on-chip SRAM, HBM, and then a large DDR capacity tier. HBM gives you bandwidth for the weights you're actively using, and the DDR tier lets you hold many models, or a very large model, resident, so you can switch between them quickly. That turns out to matter a lot for things like composition of experts or agentic workflows, where you're calling many different models in sequence.

And finally there's the multi-chip dimension. For very large models you're using tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism across sockets, and you want to map things so the communication overlaps with computation.

The nice thing about doing this in a compiler, rather than by hand-writing fused kernels, is that it generalizes. When a new model architecture comes out, a new attention variant or a different MoE routing scheme, you don't have to wait for someone to write a custom kernel. The compiler sees the dataflow graph and figures out a good spatial mapping. In practice we still do a lot of tuning for the most important models, but the fundamental approach is: think spatially, keep the data on chip, and stream it through a pipeline rather than bouncing it off memory.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it starts from the observation that the model, when you write it down in something like PyTorch, is already a dataflow graph. It's a set of operators connected by the tensors that flow between them. So the question becomes: how faithfully can the hardware represent that graph, rather than chopping it into kernels and running them one at a time through a memory hierarchy?

On a GPU, the execution model is fundamentally kernel-by-kernel. You run a matrix multiply, write the result out to HBM, read it back in for the normalization, write it out again, read it back for the attention, and so on. Every one of those round trips costs you bandwidth and latency, and for inference, especially at small batch sizes, the compute units end up sitting idle waiting on memory. People try to fix this with kernel fusion, but you can only fuse so far by hand, and every new model variant means someone has to write new fused kernels.

With a reconfigurable dataflow architecture, like what we built at SambaNova, the idea is to take a large chunk of the model graph, sometimes an entire decoder layer or multiple layers, and spatially map it onto the chip. The compiler assigns operators to compute units and configures the on-chip network and the on-chip memory so that the output of one operator flows directly into the next without touching external memory. You're essentially laying the dataflow graph out in space and then streaming data through it, so the whole thing is pipelined.

The mapping problem itself has a few dimensions. One is partitioning: deciding where to cut the graph so each section fits in the on-chip resources. Another is balancing: you want each stage of the pipeline to take roughly the same amount of time, otherwise the slow stage dictates your throughput. And then there's the memory placement: deciding which intermediate tensors live on-chip, which weights need to stream in from off-chip and when. For LLM inference the critical resource is really the weights and the KV cache, so a lot of the optimization comes down to keeping the weight bandwidth utilization high and hiding the latency of fetching the next layer's weights behind the computation of the current one.

The important thing is that this is a compiler problem, not a hand-tuning problem. The compiler sees the entire graph, it knows the shapes, it knows the hardware resources, and it can make these global decisions in a way that a human writing kernels one at a time simply cannot. That's what gets you both high utilization and low latency at the same time, which is historically a trade-off people assumed they had to make.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that you want to map the computation and the movement of data together. A model gives you a graph of operations, but inference performance depends on how you execute that graph: where the data lives, how often you move it, and how much parallelism you can exploit.

With a dataflow architecture, you can organize the hardware around that graph. You allocate compute resources to operations and arrange for intermediate results to flow directly into the operations that consume them. That creates opportunities to pipeline execution and avoid repeatedly writing intermediate results out to memory and reading them back.

The compiler is central to that process. It has to choose how to partition the graph, place operations, and use the available memory and bandwidth. And those choices depend on your objective. If you’re serving an interactive application, latency matters a great deal. If you’re processing many requests, you may optimize more for throughput. So getting the best performance means finding a mapping that balances computation, communication, and memory for the workload you actually want to run.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that you start with the computation graph of the model, and you ask how to lay that graph out spatially across the machine. Where do the operations execute, where do the weights and intermediate results live, and how does data move between them?

The important thing is to optimize those together. If you look only at how fast you can do a matrix multiply, you can miss the cost of moving data into and out of that operation. With a dataflow architecture, we can keep intermediate results on chip and stream them directly from one operation to the next. That reduces memory traffic and allows us to pipeline the computation.

Then there are tradeoffs around how much parallelism you assign to each part of the model. You want the stages to be balanced so that one stage isn’t holding up everything else. And the best mapping depends on your inference requirements—whether you’re trying to minimize latency for an individual request or maximize throughput across many requests.

So the compiler has a very important role. You want the model developer to express the model at a high level, and then have the compiler work out the placement, the memory allocation, and the communication that make efficient use of the architecture.
